# Ines Okafor — source facts and open questions

Sources read in full: `material/linkedin.md` (saved October 2026) and `material/notes.md`. These are source statements, not user-confirmed website claims. No website has been built or designed.

## Identity and approach

- Ines Okafor; Head Chef at Saltmarsh; Leeds, England, United Kingdom. Source: LinkedIn heading. Confirm formal title.
- Describes her interests as fermentation, whole-vegetable cooking and apprentices. Source: LinkedIn heading.
- Says most of what she cares about happens before service: trim, whey, stems and bones; a wall of jars and a prep list longer than the menu. Source: LinkedIn About.
- Runs the apprentice programme and writes Brine, a small zine about preserving. Source: LinkedIn About. Individual contributions and collaborators to confirm.

## Work and education

- Saltmarsh, Leeds: Head Chef, March 2022–present. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Notes say she took over the kitchen in September 2022. Relationship between these dates unresolved.
- Saltmarsh described as a 40-seat restaurant. Source: LinkedIn About. Confirm current capacity.
- Menu changes weekly. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Confirm personal responsibility and collaborators.
- Kitchen food waste reported as falling from 14 kg to 5 kg per week. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Measurement definition, baseline/end dates, method and individual/team attribution unresolved.
- Built the larder, with 40+ ferments, vinegars and garums on rotation. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Confirm count definition, timing, individual/team attribution and contributions.
- Two apprentices annually since 2023. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Confirm actual intake versus programme capacity and personal role.
- The Corn Exchange Kitchen, Leeds: Sous Chef, June 2019–February 2022. Ran the pass on a 90-cover service; took over ordering and reduced supplier list from 31 to 12. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Confirm titles, responsibilities, meaning of covers, timeframe, measurement and attribution of supplier change.
- Brassica, Manchester: Chef de Partie, September 2016–May 2019. Larder and garnish, then sauce. Source: LinkedIn Experience. Confirm formal title and personal work.
- Fjaerland Fermentation Lab, Norway: January–March 2018. Source: LinkedIn Experience. No title, activity, employment/course status or result given; overlaps Brassica. Do not infer research or any specific fermentation work from its name.
- Leeds Kitchen College: Diploma in Professional Cookery, 2014–2016. Source: LinkedIn Education.

## Other work

- Sunday Pot, Leeds: co-founder, 2021–present; a hot meal every Sunday at St Aidan's hall, cooked from restaurants' leftovers. Source: LinkedIn Volunteering. Confirm personal contribution, collaborators, current activity and which stories/material may be public.
- Brine: preserving zine, four issues, 2022–2025. Source: LinkedIn Publications. Scans available, with drawings by friend Olu. Source: notes. Confirm authorship/editing/design contributions and rights for scans and drawings.
- People ask about the jar wall, the koji room (a cupboard), staff meal and workshops on the first Monday of the month. Source: notes. Confirm workshop subject, role, venue, audience and current schedule. Do not attach a subject to the workshops based on the other topics.

## Influences

- The Art of Fermentation by Sandor Katz; Wild Fermentation; her grandmother, who never measured anything. Source: notes. No specific lesson or causal story given; ask what she wants to tell.

## Available material and rights

- About 60 dish/jar-wall photos, taken by Priya Nair for the restaurant website. Source: notes. Files not supplied here; permission to reuse, credits, restaurant rights and visible people unresolved.
- Ines's own phone photos of the larder, including labels. Source: notes. Files not supplied; employer permission, private label information and visible people unresolved.
- Scans of all four Brine issues; drawings by Olu. Source: notes. Files not supplied; ownership, collaborators' permission and credits unresolved.
- Photo of grandmother's ogiri pot. Source: notes. Photographer, permission and what it depicts beyond the pot unresolved. This does not establish that Ines makes ogiri or uses it at Saltmarsh.
- Callum Reyes, identified as Saltmarsh's owner: “Ines turned our bins into a larder. The best thing on the menu most weeks started as something we used to throw away.” Source: LinkedIn Recommendations. Permission to republish with name/title and exact wording unresolved. Treat as attributed opinion, not measured proof.

## Gaps

- Intended audience and end-of-page action; contact details and preferred contact method.
- No image files, zine scans or project documentation supplied, only descriptions.
- Personal contributions, context and evidence for claimed results.
- Day-to-day documents, rituals and terminology in Ines's own words.
- Publication boundaries and asset permissions/credits.
- Workshop details; lab role; specific influences or formative stories.
- Whether an existing personal site exists and what should happen to it.

## Disagreements

- LinkedIn dates Head Chef from March 2022; notes say kitchen takeover in September 2022. Do not select one or explain the distinction without her answer.
- Lab period overlaps Brassica employment. This may be consistent, but its relationship is unknown.

## To confirm

1. Current name, location, formal job titles and career/education dates; particularly March versus September 2022 and the Brassica/lab overlap.
2. Saltmarsh: what Ines personally changed or built, collaborators, weekly menu responsibility, and whether 40 seats remains current.
3. Waste: what 14 and 5 kg measure, when each was measured, how measured, whether comparable averages, and individual/team contribution.
4. Larder: what 40+ counts, when, and individual/team contribution; apprentices: actual annual intake versus capacity, dates and her contribution.
5. Corn Exchange: what 90 covers describes; what 31 and 12 count, timeframe, measurement and attribution; confirm personal pass/ordering role. Brassica: describe personal work.
6. Lab: position/status, actual activities and relationship to Brassica dates.
7. Sunday Pot: personal role, collaborators, whether it still operates every Sunday, and permissible stories/images.
8. Brine: personal and collaborators' roles; four issues/dates; permission to show scans and Olu's drawings, credits.
9. Workshops: subject, venue, audience, personal role and whether first-Monday schedule remains current.
10. Image permissions: Priya/restaurant images and credits; employer permission for phone photos/labels; grandmother photo photographer/rights; people/private information to omit.
11. Permission to reproduce Callum's exact quote with name/title.
12. Audience, desired visitor action and contact route.
13. What must not be shown.
14. Daily working documents, lists and rituals, with her own names for them.
15. What she learned from the named books, grandmother or other formative experiences; personal story boundaries.
16. Existing personal site and its future.

## User answers

Awaiting first fact-check response. No unanswered item is treated as approval.
# Decisions

- Keep supplied statements and confirmed claims distinct. Reason: dates, attribution and rights remain unresolved. Change by recording Ines's answers in `facts.md`.
- Keep all work in planning documents; create no implementation. Reason: explicit user instruction. Change only on a later instruction to build.
- Record asset availability without assuming reuse rights. Reason: material names photographer, illustrator and restaurant assets. Change when rights and credits are confirmed.
# Planning status

User requested a distinctive personal portfolio plan including concept, scroll narrative, contents, colour, typography, mobile behaviour and other site requirements. Explicitly no build.

Read storyfolio skill and its reading-a-profile reference. Read all supplied material: `material/linkedin.md`, `material/notes.md`.

Created `facts.md` with sourced statements, disagreements, gaps and questions. No concept, storyboard or implementation yet. First stop: user fact confirmation pending.

Next: record answers alongside relevant facts; keep skipped questions unresolved. Then read the concept reference and present three concepts with a recommendation. Following a concept choice, produce the full storyboard and requested design/practical plan. Remain within planning only.

# The concept

The second stop: from the fact sheet to three concepts the person can choose between.

## What does not work

- A new coat of paint on the same sections.
- 3D as a backdrop behind the text.
- One 3D scene, however good.
- Another site's idea with the names changed.
- A different effect for every section: a wall of jars, then a door that opens, then a scale that tips. Each may be good. Together they are a tour of effects, and nothing carries the visitor from the first to the last.

## Three things to find

**One question.** The page answers it, and the last screen gives the answer. Look where two sides of the person's work meet, or in the way from one thing to another, or in what all their projects circle. Word it as someone in HR would say it and a colleague would respect. It is about something that interests the person now, and it claims nothing the fact sheet does not hold.

Write it as a question, with a question mark. "Teardown" and "Signal from noise" are themes: they give a page a mood. A question gives the page somewhere to go, and gives the ending a job.

**One form.** A document or a ritual of the person's own trade that already runs from a beginning to an end, with section names a colleague would know: a paper, a runbook, a job card, a shift handover, a set of drawings. List at least five that the trade has, and take one the person said they work from. Its section names become the chapters, in its order, and no jokes are made in its voice. A chapter holds what its name says.

"Hero, About, Work, Skills, Contact" is the form of a website. It belongs to nobody.

**One object.** The thing that form is physically made of, in five to twelve similar pieces. The pieces carry the person's real work on their faces. They are recognisable standing together at rest. They can be built from simple shapes. They are on screen from the first screen to the last.

The object comes from what the person makes. It is not the trade's emblem: a chef's hat, a server rack, a stethoscope. For anyone who works with data, the emblem is a field of points that gathers into a chart. It fits every analyst alive, which is what is wrong with it.

## What every form has to hold

Map the form's sections onto these roles. Leave out a role that has nothing to hold. Five to eight chapters. Someone with little to show yet gets a shorter story, and not a padded one.

| Role | Holds |
|---|---|
| The opening | Their name, and the question |
| Who | Who is asking |
| Where from | The places and the years |
| How | The way they work |
| What | Some of the work shown working, then all of it |
| What came of it | Outcomes |
| What others say | Their words, one at a time |
| The close | The answer, and how to reach them |

## What the object becomes

In each chapter the same pieces take a new arrangement that shows what the chapter is about: the way they came as a line or a map, how they work as a diagram, one piece of work as an exhibit, every project as a wall whose faces carry real pictures, outcomes as cards. At the close the object is whole again.

If a chapter's 3D could be deleted and only decoration would be lost, the pieces are not showing that chapter yet.

**The opening shows where the object comes from.** The answer is the person's own: what they learned from, or what they began with. The object may gather, be put together, unfold, be drawn, develop or switch on.

## Three concepts, each written like this

Make three that differ in kind: in their form or their object, and not in their colour. Write them to `docs/story/concepts.md`.

- **The question.**
- **The form,** with each chapter's name and the role it holds.
- **The object,** and its pieces.
- **What it becomes** in three of the chapters.
- **The opening and the close.**
- **What it stands on:** the lines of the fact sheet it needs.
- **What it needs from the person:** a picture, someone else's yes.
- **Why it is theirs:** one sentence on why it could not sit on a colleague's site.

Then say which you would choose, and why.

## Test each one before you show it

Rework or drop one that fails.

| Test | Ask |
|---|---|
| Swap | Could it sit unchanged on a colleague's site? Then it is not theirs yet. |
| Backdrop | With the 3D deleted, is meaning lost, or only decoration? |
| Depth | Has it a beginning, a middle and an end that follow from one another? |
| Emblem | Is the object the picture that stands for the job? |
| Honesty | Does any sentence in it say more than the fact sheet does: a ranking, a reason, which came first, how a thing was left, a day, a place? |
| Thirty seconds | Can someone who does not scroll get the name, the work, some proof, and how to reach them? |

## Three cases

How each was reasoned, and not only where it ended.

**A research paper.** The site this skill came from belongs to someone whose work lies between AI research and software engineering. Three restyled layouts were, in their words, "all cliche". Three single 3D scenes were "not deep enough". What turned it was a sentence of theirs: "Think of it like a research question." The form became a paper, with a paper's chapters: Abstract, Introduction, Background, Method, Experiments, Results, Peer review, Conclusion. The object became the paper's nine pages, which fold into a globe for where they have lived, stand as the layers of a network for how they work, and hang as a wall of projects. The question was first too abstract for a recruiter, and was reworded. The opening was first a plain pile of pages. It became the front pages of the papers they learned from, gathering into the paper as the reader scrolls.

**A tasting menu.** Camille is a pastry chef, made up for this page. She trained in Lyon, spent six years in the pastry sections of two restaurants, and now runs a dessert-only evening once a month: 24 seats, five courses, all sweet. People write to her about one burnt-honey tart. Her trade's forms: the recipe card, the prep list, the tasting menu, the order sheet, the costing sheet. She serves in courses and plans by the menu, so the form is a tasting menu, and each course is a chapter. Each course arrives on a plate, so the object is a stack of plates. The question: "What makes someone remember a dessert?" Turned down first: a whisk and a chef's hat turning in the air, which is the emblem, and one croissant in 3D, which is one scene.

**An incident review.** Jun is a reliability engineer, also made up. Seven years on call, at a payments company and then at one that books hospital appointments. He wrote his team's incident review template, and gives talks on reviews without blame. His trade's forms: the runbook, the incident review, the on-call handover, the status page, the dashboard. His work is what happens after something breaks, so the form is an incident review: summary, timeline, root cause, action items. A status page is made of tiles, one to a service, so the object is those tiles. The question: "What keeps a system up at 3 a.m.?" Turned down first: a server rack turning, which is the emblem, and a globe of pings behind the text, which is a backdrop.

**An example shows how to reason. Its concept is not taken.** Camille's menu was reasoned from how Camille serves. A chef who sells one loaf a day from a hatch is not a tasting menu. If you find one of these three concepts in your hand for someone else, it has already failed the swap test: it was made for a person who is not in front of you.

In this version a concept is shown in words. There is no engine yet to sketch one on.
# Asking

## Facts

At the first stop your questions go in one message, numbered. `reading-a-profile.md` says what they are.

## A choice

Where you offer a choice, the concept above all, give the ones you would not choose as fully as the one you would. Then say which you would choose, and why.

If the person tells you to choose, choose. Write what you chose, and what you chose it over, into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.

## If the person will not answer

Some people will not answer your questions, or will say: decide everything. Then:

- **What is a matter of taste, you decide:** the concept, the look, the order. Say which you chose and what you chose it over.
- **A fact, you do not decide.** What you could not confirm stays off the page. A figure whose meaning you do not know, a project you cannot say ever ran, a paper you cannot say they wrote, a title you cannot say is theirs: leave it out, or carry it in the script marked "to confirm", and stand nothing on it. Build the concept on the facts that needed no confirming. The person's own resume is no exception: if you asked whether a project ever ran and they did not say, "real-time system" is still not confirmed, and it is not printed.
- **Say what is waiting on them,** as a numbered list at the top of what you hand over.

A wrong guess about someone's taste costs them an afternoon. A wrong claim about their work is read by the people they most want to convince, and it is their name on the site, not yours.

# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

# Three concepts and the chosen direction

## Pending facts and assets

1. Contact route and workshop booking details.
2. Authentic redacted prep/log excerpts and own photos, not yet supplied as files.
3. Restaurant permission for Priya's photos; Olu permission for his drawings. Neither assumed.

User authorized judgement on unanswered matters. Choose taste; omit unresolved factual claims. Source basis: facts.md, especially user corrections.

## Forms considered

Ferment log, prep list, recipe sheet, ordering sheet, weekly menu, shift handover. Only the log and prep list are confirmed daily tools. Menu confirmed as the last document written each week. Others are trade possibilities, not claims about Ines.

## A — The ferment log (chosen)

- Question: What happens before the menu is written?
- Form: log, using confirmed fields in order: Started (opening/who/origin), Salt (how), Checks (work/process), Ready (outcome), then Closed log / Menu (answer/contact). These are editorial chapters derived from fields, not a claim about her exact template.
- Object: eight paper leaves in one bound ferment log. This is a proposed visual representation of her real log, not an assertion it is a paper notebook. Simple page planes, shallow cover and binding; real redacted excerpts and own images on faces.
- Transformations: Started opens cover to the grandmother's pot photo and current role; Salt fans leaves to expose the log's fields; Checks aligns leaves along actual check entries; Ready pairs measured kitchen outcome with its definition; Menu reunites all eight leaves into the closed log beside audience-specific contact paths.
- Opening: log opens to her own photo of grandmother's ogiri pot and attribution as a stated influence. No invented lesson, childhood story or recipe connection.
- Close: log comes together; menu-written-last fact answers the question. Routes for apprentices, workshop enquiries and writers.
- Stands on: confirmed daily log fields/menu order; own pot/larder images; corrected title; stage tasks; confirmed waste attribution and scope; approved Callum quote.
- Needs: own photos and actual redacted log/prep excerpts; contact destinations. Priya/Olu material optional, never required.
- Why theirs: the relationship between her dated/checkable ferment log and her menu-written-last practice carries the page, with her pot photograph and whole-kitchen evidence.

## B — The prep list

- Question: What does the menu leave out?
- Form: prep list; proposed editorial groups: Before service (opening), Prep (who/how), Larder (work), Check (process), Ready for service (outcomes), Next list (close). These group names need not be represented as her actual list headings.
- Object: six paper slips clipped together as one list; every slip carries one real redacted list excerpt or owned photo. No invented task is ticked complete.
- Transformations: Prep unfolds the clipped list; Larder spreads slips as an index of actual excerpt/photo pairs; Check aligns selected tasks with authentic log entries; close clips them together.
- Opening: her list and own pot photo establish present practice and stated influence without claiming a causal story.
- Close: complete list, then menu-last fact and contact paths.
- Stands on: confirmed prep-list practice, log fields, menu-last order, own images, corrected role and waste facts.
- Needs: actual list excerpt and confirmation of any task labels; same contact/assets as A.
- Why theirs: it foregrounds her explicit distinction between the long prep list and the last-written menu.
- Tradeoff: task completion can suggest a verified sequence that we do not yet have; its progression is less grounded than the named log fields.

## C — The jar record

- Question: How do you know when a jar is ready?
- Form: ferment log fields: Started (opening/who), Salt (method), Check days (process), Ready (work), Record closed (outcome/contact).
- Object: six jar-and-label units as one small larder shelf. Labels are the physical carriers of selected log records, a proposed visualization rather than a claim she stores the full log on jars. Simple cylinders and flat label faces; no simulated fermentation.
- Transformations: Started lifts labels into readable view; Checks arranges the same jars by genuine check entries; Ready reunites shelf with the actual ready records displayed. No invented jar names, salt ratios or times.
- Opening: her pot photo beside the emerging shelf; no assertion the pot recipe became any jar's contents.
- Close: shelf reunites and links to learning/workshop/writer enquiries. It does not claim a universal method for judging readiness.
- Stands on: confirmed jar/log practice, real larder photos and future authentic excerpts.
- Needs: several real complete jar records, own photos and readiness explanations; no inferred food safety advice.
- Why theirs: labels show her actual dates, salt and checking practice, rather than generic glass decoration.
- Tradeoff: requires more missing records and risks visitors mistaking an edited record for a recipe. Glass also costs more to render well on phones.

## Selection

A chosen by assistant under user's explicit judgement instruction. It uses the most complete confirmed sequence, keeps readable records as the 3D substance and can include teaching/publication enquiries without pretending those activities are stages in a recipe. Prefer A over B's unverified task order and C's record/recipe risk and heavier rendering.

## Checks

All concepts: object persists from first to last; content sits on faces, not behind them; first screen has identity, activity, a real evidence preview and contact jump. One ordinary HTML narrative duplicates the evidence so that loss of 3D loses the spatial explanation, not access to information. No unverified metrics/roles, invented jar records, causal waste claim, paid-work claim for stage, current workshop schedule or unapproved artwork.

| Shared link/icon | Build | Assistant: factual name/role description, log-page thumbnail, simple ruled-page icon; cleared image only |

| Blog | Later | Assistant: only if Ines wants an ongoing writing workflow |

| Writer contact | Build | Assistant: contact and factual short bio; downloadable assets later with rights/credits |

| Search/accessibility/performance | Build | Assistant: semantic indexed HTML, metadata, canonical URL once known, sitemap, 404, keyboard/zoom/device checks |

One scene and the same eight leaves throughout. Lazy-load optional 3D after useful HTML renders; pause rendering when offscreen, tab hidden or scene settled. Phone defaults to simpler presentation; load scene only where it can run smoothly.

Future acceptance: reading/contact work with no JS and no WebGL; reduced-motion has no camera/page travel; all links/controls work by keyboard/touch; text survives 200% zoom; no scroll traps; correct team attribution/time/scope beside waste figures; Fjaerland never framed as research; excluded prices/faces absent; credits and approvals complete. Test a modest phone and desktop; target Core Web Vitals LCP <=2.5 s, INP <=200 ms, CLS <=0.1. These are targets, not measured results.

Assistant chose concept A, light palette, typography, six-chapter order, eight-leaf visual representation, mobile simplification, English and direct enquiry routes. Paper log is a design metaphor; exact log format is unknown. Nothing about recipes, workshop topics, vacancies, ongoing waste performance or unconfirmed achievements assumed.

Ask Ines to accept storyboard or name changes. Caption writing and building remain outside this planning version. No acceptance has yet been recorded.

I’ve chosen **the ferment log** as the site’s central idea. The page asks: **“What happens before the menu is written?”** Your own practice supplies the answer.

The full plan is in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-pLveBf/docs/story/storyboard.md). Nothing has been built.

**Still needed:** your contact and workshop destinations, selected own photos, and authentic redacted log/prep-list excerpts. Priya’s photos remain conditional on restaurant permission; Olu’s drawings remain conditional on his permission.

### The idea

One 3D log, made of eight paper leaves, stays with the visitor throughout. Its pages open, spread into readable records, show evidence, then close again. The movement reveals your work rather than sitting behind it.

I considered a prep-list concept and a jar-record concept too. I chose the log because its confirmed fields give the story a clear sequence, and it needs fewer missing facts. All three are documented in [concepts.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-pLveBf/docs/story/concepts.md).

### From top to bottom

| Part | What it shows | What moves |
|---|---|---|
| **Started** | Your name, role, Leeds, and your grandmother’s pot as a stated influence | The log opens to your own photograph |
| **Salt** | The log’s actual fields and your prep-list practice | Pages fan out to expose a real, redacted excerpt |
| **Checks** | Larder evidence and the modest, precise account of your unpaid stage | Pages arrange into readable rows |
| **Ready** | The whole-kitchen waste result, with “we,” the 2023 measurement period and exclusions | Two pages become paired evidence panels |
| **Log note** | Callum’s approved quote, clearly attributed | One page turns forward |
| **Menu** | Your statement that the menu is written last; apprentice, writer and workshop enquiry routes | The same pages reunite into the closed log |

Visitors can jump directly to any chapter or contact route. The first screen carries your identity, an evidence preview and a contact link.

### Colour and type

Warm paper **#F3EFE5**, charcoal **#242820**, deep olive **#46543A**. Matte surfaces, restrained shadows and your photographs supply the texture.

**Source Serif 4** carries the narrative; **IBM Plex Mono** carries log fields and dates. Actual handwriting stays in source images, with readable transcripts.

### On a phone

A single-column story with compact log illustrations replaces the long pinned scene. Images and records open at readable sizes; contact remains easy to reach.

Reduced motion uses static arrangements. Without WebGL or JavaScript, visitors still get the complete text, images, evidence and links. Scrolling remains native throughout.

### What else it needs

The plan includes chapter navigation, three enquiry routes, image credits, accessible transcripts, sharing metadata, a site icon, a useful 404 page, applicable privacy information and a simple content-update process. Workshop booking initially links to your supplied destination. Blog, project pages and analytics can wait until there is a clear need.

I assumed the **paper format**, eight leaves, visual style and enquiry structure. I did not assume recipes, workshop subjects, vacancies, unconfirmed achievements or a cause for the waste reduction. These choices are recorded in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-pLveBf/docs/story/decided-for-you.md).

Does this storyboard feel right, or what would you change?

The [storyfolio skill](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-with-pLveBf/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) requires “a yes to the script, or what to change.” This is the final planning review; building remains outside this task.
